items.hint1: Focus on the words “non-permanent member”. That label only makes sense in a body where some other members keep their seats permanently.
items.hint2: Nigeria has belonged to the continental bodies and to the oil exporters’ club for decades, so it could not be newly admitted to them in 2014. OPEC also has no permanent or non-permanent seats.
items.hint3: Of the world body and the continental body, which one has a council where five countries hold their seats permanently and the rest are elected for two years?
items.solution:
Answer: A. United Nations (UN)

“Non-permanent member” is a term from the UN Security Council. The Council has five permanent members (the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China) and ten non-permanent members, elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.

How to tell: Nigeria was elected in October 2013 and sat on the Security Council as a non-permanent member for 2014 and 2015. The word “non-permanent” points to a body that also has permanent members, and among these options that is the UN.

Why not the others:
B. African Union (AU): Nigeria has been a member since the AU was formed in 2002, and the AU has no permanent members.
C. Organization of African Unity (OAU): Nigeria was a founding member in 1963, and the OAU was replaced by the AU in 2002, so it did not exist in 2014.
D. Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC): Nigeria joined in 1971, and OPEC has no permanent or non-permanent seats.

Exam tip: when a question says “permanent” or “non-permanent member”, think of the UN Security Council first. Then check the year: a body Nigeria joined decades earlier, or one that had already ended, cannot be where it was newly admitted.

items.hint1: Many Hausa titles begin with “Sarkin”, meaning “head of” or “chief of”. The word after it tells you which group or area the official was in charge of.
items.hint2: The Waziri was the Emir’s chief adviser, a bit like a prime minister, so he did not lead any trade group. “Fada” means the palace, so that title is about palace affairs.
items.hint3: Two titles remain. One is linked with water and fishing, the other with meat. Which word goes with meat?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Sarkin Pawa

In the Hausa-Fulani emirate system, the Emir ruled through appointed officials, each in charge of one area of life. Heads of trade and craft groups carried the title “Sarkin” followed by the name of their group, and the Sarkin Pawa was the head of all butchers.

How to tell: read the word after “Sarkin”. Pawa is linked with butchers and meat, so the Sarkin Pawa led the butchers.

Why not the others:
A. Sarkin Fada: he was the head of the palace officials and palace affairs.
B. Sarkin Ruwa: he was in charge of water matters, the river and fishing.
D. Waziri: he was the Emir’s chief adviser, like a prime minister, not the head of a trade group.

Exam tip: learn Hausa titles as pairs of title and duty: Waziri (chief adviser), Galadima (in charge of the capital), Madawaki (army commander), Alkali (judge), Sarkin Fada (palace), Sarkin Ruwa (water and fishing), Sarkin Pawa (butchers). For a “Sarkin” title, the word after it usually names the area.

items.hint1: Each military regime in Nigeria gave its highest ruling body a name. Link the body’s name to the regime that created it.
items.hint2: The Supreme Military Council was the name used by the regimes from 1966 up to 1985, and the Provisional Ruling Council was the name used from 1993.
items.hint3: The AFRC was set up in August 1985 after a palace coup. Of the leaders left, who came to power that year?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Ibrahim Babangida

When Ibrahim Babangida took power in August 1985, he replaced the Supreme Military Council with a new top body, the Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC). It made the main decisions of his regime until he stepped aside in 1993.

How to tell: match the body to the year. AFRC means 1985, and 1985 means Babangida, who removed Buhari.

Why not the others:
A. Sani Abacha: his highest body was the Provisional Ruling Council (PRC), from 1993.
C. Muhammadu Buhari: his highest body, from 1983 to 1985, was the Supreme Military Council, and the 1985 coup that created the AFRC removed him.
D. Yakubu Gowon: his highest body, from 1966 to 1975, was the Supreme Military Council.

Exam tip: learn the ruling bodies as a timeline: Supreme Military Council (Ironsi, Gowon, Murtala and Obasanjo, Buhari), AFRC (Babangida), PRC (Abacha and Abubakar). A question on one body is then a question on one period.

items.hint1: Think about which of these countries actually had atomic bombs in the early 1960s. A country without the bomb cannot test one.
items.hint2: Chad and Libya had no atomic bombs to test. Nigeria’s break with Israel came in 1973, over a war in the Middle East.
items.hint3: Two remain. Which of them ruled Algeria in 1960, when the bombs were tested in the Algerian part of the Sahara?
items.solution:
Answer: A. France

In 1960 France tested its first atomic bombs in the Sahara Desert, in Algeria, which it then ruled. The Balewa government saw this as a danger to Africans and an insult to African opinion, and in January 1961 it broke diplomatic relations with France.

How to tell: only a country with atomic bombs could carry out the tests, and France was the power testing them in the Sahara in 1960 and 1961.

Why not the others:
B. Israel: Nigeria broke relations with Israel in 1973, in support of Arab and African states after the Arab-Israeli war, not over bomb tests.
C. Chad: it is Nigeria’s neighbour and had no atomic bomb to test.
D. Libya: it had no atomic bomb and carried out no tests in the Sahara.

Exam tip: link each break in relations to its cause: France in 1961 over atomic tests in the Sahara, Israel in 1973 over the Arab-Israeli war. The cause in the question tells you the country.

items.hint1: Nigeria’s states were created in stages. Recall how many states each stage produced, and in which year.
items.hint2: One option is a year long before Nigeria existed, and in another Nigeria still had regions, not states.
items.hint3: The move from 12 states to 19 was made by the Murtala Mohammed regime. Which remaining year falls in his short time in power?
items.solution:
Answer: B. 1976

In February 1976 the Murtala Mohammed regime created seven new states from the existing twelve, bringing Nigeria to 19 states. The aim was to answer demands from groups who felt left out and to bring government closer to the people.

How to tell: follow the ladder of state creation.
1963: the Mid-West Region is created, making four regions
1967: 12 states (Gowon)
1976: 19 states (Murtala Mohammed)
1987: 21 states (Babangida)
1991: 30 states (Babangida)
1996: 36 states (Abacha)

Why not the others:
A. 1967: this is when Gowon created the first 12 states.
C. 1789: this is more than a century before Nigeria was formed in 1914.
D. 1965: Nigeria still had four regions then, not states.

Exam tip: memorise the ladder 12, 19, 21, 30, 36 with its years and rulers. Any state-creation question, whether it gives the number, the year or the ruler, can be answered from it.

items.hint1: Think about how many parties were allowed in each Nigerian republic, and whether politicians or the government formed them.
items.hint2: The First Republic had several competing parties, such as the NPC, NCNC and AG, and so did the Second Republic, with the NPN, UPN, NPP, GNPP and PRP.
items.hint3: Two remain. Which one came from the Babangida transition programme, when the government itself formed the parties and built their offices?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Third Republic

Under Babangida’s transition programme, the government refused to register the parties formed by politicians and instead created two parties of its own in 1989: the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and the National Republican Convention (NRC). Every politician had to join one of the two. The republic was never fully completed, because the presidential election of 12 June 1993 was annulled.

How to tell: two government-made parties, the SDP and NRC, belong to the Third Republic.

Why not the others:
A. First Republic: it had several parties, such as the NPC, NCNC, AG and NEPU.
B. Second Republic: it had five parties at first, the NPN, UPN, NPP, GNPP and PRP.
D. Fourth Republic: it began in 1999 with three parties, the PDP, APP and AD, and has had many registered parties since.

Exam tip: link each republic to its party system: First and Second, multi-party; Third, two parties created by government; Fourth, multi-party. A question naming the SDP or NRC is about the Third Republic.

items.hint1: This is a “not” question. OPEC is a group of countries that earn much of their income from selling crude oil, so look for the country that does not fit.
items.hint2: Venezuela and Kuwait were among the five countries that founded OPEC in Baghdad in 1960.
items.hint3: Two African countries remain. Which one has earned most of its export income from crude oil for decades?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Uganda

OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, is made up of countries whose economies depend heavily on exporting crude oil. It was founded in 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. Uganda is not a member.

How to tell: check each country against the list of members. Venezuela and Kuwait are founding members, and Nigeria joined in 1971. Uganda has not joined.

Why not the others:
B. Venezuela: it is one of the five founding members of 1960.
C. Nigeria: it joined OPEC in 1971 and is one of its main African members.
D. Kuwait: it is one of the five founding members of 1960.

Exam tip: learn the five founders (Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela) and the African members, such as Nigeria, Algeria, Libya, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Congo. An African country missing from that list is the likely non-member.

items.hint1: The bag got its nickname from a real event in which many people had to leave Nigeria in a hurry. Find the year of that event first, then ask who was ruling Ghana in that year.
items.hint2: Ghana’s first leader lost power in 1966, and the leader who became president in 2001 came far too late.
items.hint3: Two leaders remain. One expelled Nigerians from Ghana in 1969. The other ruled Ghana when Nigeria’s Shagari government sent out illegal immigrants in 1983. Which event gave the bag its name?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Jerry John Rawlings

In January 1983 the Shagari government ordered illegal immigrants, most of them Ghanaians, to leave Nigeria within about two weeks. Many packed their things into large, cheap woven bags, and the bags became known as “Ghana Must Go”. At that time Ghana was ruled by Jerry Rawlings, who had taken power at the end of 1981.

How to tell: fix the event (the 1983 expulsion), then the year (1983), then who ruled Ghana in that year (Rawlings).

Why not the others:
A. Kwame Nkrumah: he was removed from power in 1966, long before 1983.
C. Kofi Abrefa Busia: his 1969 Aliens Compliance Order sent many Nigerians out of Ghana and is often seen as the background, but the bag and its name come from 1983.
D. John Agyekum Kufuor: he was president from 2001 to 2009, long after the bag got its name.

Exam tip: when a question links an event to a foreign leader, first pin down the year of the event, then find who ruled that country in that year. Do not pick a leader because they are linked to an earlier, similar event.

items.hint1: Separate the jobs involved: deciding the policy, carrying it out, approving treaties, and settling legal disputes. The question asks who decides it.
items.hint2: The courts interpret laws, and the National Assembly mainly approves treaties and confirms ambassadors. Neither of them draws up the policy.
items.hint3: Both remaining options belong to the executive arm. Read each one to the very end, and ask which one describes where the final decision is taken.
items.solution:
Answer: A. The Executive (President and Federal Executive Council)

In Nigeria’s presidential system, foreign policy is decided mainly by the executive: the President, working with the Federal Executive Council, which is made up of the ministers. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs advises them and carries the policy out through Nigeria’s embassies.

How to tell: “formulation” means deciding what the policy will be. That decision rests with the President and the Federal Executive Council.

Why not the others:
B. The National Assembly: it checks foreign policy, for example by passing a treaty into Nigerian law and by the Senate confirming ambassadors, but it does not draw it up.
C. The Judiciary: it interprets laws and settles disputes, and plays no part in planning relations with other countries.
D. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs alone: the ministry advises and carries out the policy, but it answers to the President and the Council, so “alone” makes this wrong.

Exam tip: in “who does it” questions, separate the stages: the executive formulates, the legislature approves or checks, and a ministry implements. Watch for words such as “alone” or “only”, which can turn a partly true option into a wrong one.

items.hint1: Look at the key word in the question: “right”. Some of these terms describe strength or the ability to force people, while others describe a recognised right.
items.hint2: Power is the ability to make people obey, even by force, and it can exist without any right. Legitimacy is the people’s acceptance that a ruler is rightful, which supports the right but is not the right itself.
items.hint3: Two remain. One stresses the supremacy and independence of the state. The other is about a recognised right to command. Which fits the stem’s word “right”?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Authority

Authority is the recognised or lawful right to give orders and to be obeyed. It is often described as power plus legitimacy: power that the people accept as rightful.

How to tell: the stem says “the right to enforce obedience”. In Government, the term defined as a right to command is authority.

Why not the others:
B. Sovereignty: it is the supreme power of the state to make and enforce laws, free from outside control, so it stresses supremacy and independence rather than a right to be obeyed.
C. Power: it is the ability or capacity to make people obey, which can exist without any right, as an armed robber shows.
D. Legitimacy: it is the people’s acceptance that a government’s power is rightful, which turns power into authority but is not itself the right to command.

Exam tip: match the key word to the term: “ability” or “capacity” points to power, “right” points to authority, “acceptance” points to legitimacy, and “supreme” or “independent” points to sovereignty.

items.hint1: This question has an “All of the above” option. Test each of the first three statements on its own and ask whether it is true.
items.hint2: The Federal Character Commission enforces the federal character principle, which says that appointments should reflect Nigeria’s different states and groups so that no one section dominates.
items.hint3: Look at your results. If two or more of the first three statements are true, can any single one of them be the full answer?
items.solution:
Answer: D. All of the above

The Federal Character Commission, set up in 1996 and written into the 1999 Constitution, enforces the federal character principle. That principle requires that appointments to government and its agencies reflect Nigeria’s different states and groups, to promote national unity and to stop any section from dominating the rest.

How to tell: each statement is part of that purpose.
A describes fair shares of appointments.
B describes unity by preventing domination by one section.
C describes keeping smaller groups from being shut out.
Since all three are true, the full answer is all of them.

Why not the others:
A. Ensure equitable representation of different ethnic groups in government appointments: true, but it is only one part of the purpose.
B. Promote national unity by reducing sectional dominance: true, but it is only one part of the purpose.
C. Prevent marginalization of minority groups in public service: true, but it is only one part of the purpose.

Exam tip: with an “All of the above” option, check the other options one by one. If you find two true and none false, choose “All of the above”. If even one is false, rule it out.

items.hint1: Notice the time clue “during the colonial era”. The question asks for the name of the system of rule in that period.
items.hint2: One option is the movement Africans used to fight against foreign rule, and one describes indirect control that came after independence.
items.hint3: Two remain. One is the broad drive of a powerful country to spread its control over others by many means. The other is the direct rule and exploitation of a colony. Which matches the colonial era?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Colonialism

Colonialism is the direct political control of a territory by a foreign power, which then uses the territory’s land, labour and resources for its own benefit. The “colonial era” in Africa is simply the period when this system was in force.

How to tell: the stem gives both marks of colonialism, economic exploitation and political subjugation (being ruled by others), and places them in the colonial era.

Why not the others:
B. Imperialism: it is the broader policy or drive of a powerful nation to extend its control over others, and colonialism is its direct form in the colonial era.
C. Neocolonialism: it is indirect control, mainly economic, that continues after a country becomes independent.
D. Nationalism: it is the movement that rose to fight against colonial rule, not the rule itself.

Exam tip: use time clues. “During the colonial era” points to colonialism, “after independence” points to neocolonialism, and a broad “extending power over other nations” points to imperialism.

items.hint1: Decide whether the stem describes a country’s overall dealings with the world, a method used in those dealings, a set of rules, or a process affecting the whole world.
items.hint2: International law is the body of rules that govern how states relate, and globalization is the worldwide linking of economies and cultures, not one country’s conduct.
items.hint3: Two remain. One is a tool, mainly negotiation through ambassadors. The other is the country’s whole plan and conduct towards other states. Which one is the interaction itself?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Foreign policy

Foreign policy is the set of goals and actions that guide a country’s dealings with other countries. Government texts commonly define it as the totality of a country’s interactions with other states in international politics.

How to tell: the stem asks for a country’s interaction in international politics as a whole, which is its foreign policy.

Why not the others:
B. Diplomacy: it is the method, mainly negotiation through ambassadors, used to carry out foreign policy, not the interaction as a whole.
C. International law: it is the body of rules that govern relations between states.
D. Globalization: it is the worldwide process that links economies and cultures, not one country’s own conduct.

Exam tip: foreign policy is the “what”, the plan and conduct of a country’s relations, and diplomacy is the “how”, the tool used to carry it out. When the stem speaks of a country’s overall dealings, choose foreign policy.

items.hint1: Recall the ladder of state creation in Nigeria and the ruler behind each step.
items.hint2: Gowon created the first 12 states in 1967, and Babangida raised the number to 21 in 1987 and then to 30 in 1991.
items.hint3: Two remain. The six new states that made 36 were announced in October 1996. Which of the two was in power that year?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Sani Abacha

In October 1996 the Abacha regime created six new states, raising the number from 30 to 36. This is the structure Nigeria still has, along with the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.

How to tell: follow the ladder.
1967: 12 states (Gowon)
1976: 19 states (Murtala Mohammed)
1987: 21 states (Babangida)
1991: 30 states (Babangida)
1996: 36 states (Abacha)

Why not the others:
B. Yakubu Gowon: he created the first 12 states in 1967.
C. Ibrahim Babangida: he took Nigeria to 21 states and then 30, not 36.
D. Olusegun Obasanjo: no new states were created in either of his periods in power, 1976 to 1979 and 1999 to 2007.

Exam tip: keep one ladder of number, year and ruler for state creation. Most questions on this topic give one of the three and ask for another.

items.hint1: A colony also has people and land. Ask what an independent state has that a colony lacks.
items.hint2: Nigeria before 1960 already had a large population and a clear territory, yet it was not independent, so neither of those made it independent.
items.hint3: Two remain. One is a document that sets out how the government works. The other is supreme power that no outside body can overrule. Which is the mark of independence?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Sovereignty

Sovereignty is the supreme power of a state to make and enforce its own laws, free from outside control. A territory that has it governs itself, so other states recognise it as independent.

How to tell: before 1 October 1960, Nigeria had people, land and even constitutions, but Britain had the final say. At independence Nigeria gained sovereignty, and with it, recognition as an independent state.

Why not the others:
A. Population: a colony has people too, so a population does not make a state independent.
B. Territory: a colony has land too, so territory alone does not make a state independent.
D. Constitution: colonies had constitutions as well, such as Nigeria’s constitutions of 1922 to 1954, so a constitution does not prove independence.

Exam tip: population, territory, government and sovereignty are all features of a state, but when the question is about independence or freedom from outside control, the feature is sovereignty.

items.hint1: Look at who the members of these bodies are: individual citizens, political parties, or whole countries.
items.hint2: Pressure groups are groups of citizens trying to influence a government, so they do not have countries as their members.
items.hint3: ECOWAS began as an economic community, but the OAU and AU deal mainly with unity and peace. Of the labels left, which one fits every body on the list?
items.solution:
Answer: C. International organizations

An international organization is a body formed by two or more sovereign states to work together on shared aims. ECOWAS, the OAU and the AU are all made up of member countries, so they are international organizations.

How to tell: ECOWAS (founded 1975) has West African states as its members. The OAU (founded 1963) and the AU, which replaced it in 2002, have African states as their members. All are bodies of countries.

Why not the others:
A. Political institutions: these are organs inside one country’s political system, such as the legislature, the executive and the courts.
B. Economic organizations: this fits ECOWAS’s main aim, but not the OAU and AU, whose main aims are political.
D. Pressure groups: these are groups of citizens that try to influence a government, not unions of countries.

Exam tip: when a question lists several bodies and asks what they are, pick the label that fits every one of them. A label that fits only one item on the list is a trap.

items.hint1: Look at the list as a whole. Which school subject studies how states are ruled, how power is organised and how parties compete for it?
items.hint2: Sociology studies society and social groups in general, and Civic Education teaches the rights, duties and values of a good citizen.
items.hint3: Two remain, and both look at colonisation and decolonisation. Which one treats party systems and constitutions as its main subject, rather than as events in the story of the past?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Government

Government, as a school subject, studies the state, how power is organised and used, and how people take part in politics. Military rule, party systems, political parties, constitutional development, colonisation and decolonisation are all topics in the Government syllabus.

How to tell: the list covers systems of rule (military rule), how parties compete (party systems, political parties) and how the state’s rules developed (constitutional development). Together these are the subject matter of Government.

Why not the others:
A. Civic Education: it teaches citizens’ rights, duties and values, not party systems or constitutional development.
B. Sociology: it studies society, families and social groups in general.
D. History: it covers colonisation and decolonisation as past events, but party systems and political parties as topics of study belong to Government.

Exam tip: when a question lists topics and asks which subject covers them, pick the subject that covers every item on the list, not one that shares just one or two.

items.hint1: For each job named, think about which person or body carries it out under the 1999 Constitution.
items.hint2: Elections in Nigeria are conducted by INEC, the Independent National Electoral Commission, not by the President.
items.hint3: Three remain. For each, ask who chose that official in the first place, because the power to remove usually goes with the power to choose.
items.solution:
Answer: A. Appoint ministers

Under the 1999 Constitution, the President appoints the ministers who form the Federal Executive Council, subject to confirmation by the Senate, and must choose at least one minister from each state.

How to tell: ministers are chosen by the President, so appointing them is a presidential power. The officials in the other options are chosen by the voters or handled by INEC.

Why not the others:
B. Conduct elections: this is the job of INEC, an independent body.
C. Appoint governors: state governors are elected by the voters of their states.
D. Recall senators: a senator can be recalled only by the voters of the senatorial district, through a petition and a vote run by INEC.

Exam tip: for “the President has the power to” questions, ask who chose the official. If the voters elect the official, the President cannot appoint or recall them. If the President appoints, as with ministers, the Senate usually confirms.

items.hint1: Picture what happens when soldiers take over: what becomes of elections, political parties and the legislature?
items.hint2: Military rulers often claim they seized power to protect national security, and a person’s ethnic identity comes by birth, which a change of government does not remove.
items.hint3: Two remain. Think back to what you pictured in hint 1, and ask which one is directly removed when those things are suspended.
items.solution:
Answer: C. Political participation

Political participation means citizens taking part in choosing their leaders and influencing government, by voting, contesting elections, joining parties and campaigning. Military regimes suspend the constitution, ban parties, dissolve the legislature and rule by decree, which takes these ways of taking part away from citizens.

How to tell: under military rule there are no elections and no parties, so citizens cannot choose or remove their rulers. That goes against political participation.

Why not the others:
A. National security: military rulers often give it as their reason for seizing power, so it is not something they reject.
B. Ethnic identity: it is who a person is by birth, not a principle of government, and military rule does not remove it.
D. Conflict resolution: military regimes still settle disputes, even if often by force, so it is not the principle they negate.

Exam tip: when a question asks what military rule “negates” or “violates”, look for a democratic principle: political participation, the rule of law, separation of powers or constitutionalism.

items.hint1: Nigeria moved from regions to states in stages. Pin down the first time regions were replaced by states.
items.hint2: In 1965 Nigeria still had four regions, and 1979 is the year the Second Republic began, not a year when states were created.
items.hint3: Two remain. Gowon announced the 12 states just before the Nigerian Civil War began. In which of the two years did the war start?
items.solution:
Answer: B. 1967

On 27 May 1967 General Yakubu Gowon replaced Nigeria’s four regions with 12 states. One aim was to weaken the Eastern Region’s move to break away and to answer the demands of minority groups.

How to tell: follow the ladder of state creation.
1963: four regions, after the Mid-West is created
1967: 12 states (Gowon)
1976: 19 states (Murtala Mohammed)

Why not the others:
A. 1976: this is when the 12 states became 19.
C. 1979: this is when the Second Republic began, and Nigeria still had 19 states.
D. 1965: Nigeria still had four regions and no states.

Exam tip: 1967 is the year Nigeria first had states. It also saw the start of the civil war, so link the two dates together in your memory.

items.hint1: Sovereignty is a feature of every independent state, whatever its form of government. Look for the option that would be true of any independent state.
items.hint2: Tyranny is the cruel misuse of power by a ruler, and a colony is by definition ruled from outside, so neither describes sovereignty.
items.hint3: Two remain. Test each on a state you know, such as Nigeria, which is a federation. Does the option still hold?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Supremacy and independence of the state

Sovereignty has two sides. Inside the state, its power is supreme, so no person or group within it can overrule its laws. Outside, the state is independent, so no foreign power controls it.

How to tell: the option that names both sides, supremacy and independence, describes sovereignty and holds for every independent state.

Why not the others:
B. Act of tyranny of an independent state: tyranny is the abuse of power, not what sovereignty means.
C. Use of a strong army in a unitary state: sovereignty does not depend on army size, and federal states such as Nigeria are sovereign too.
D. Group interest in a colonial state: a colony is ruled from outside, so it lacks sovereignty.

Exam tip: when asked what sovereignty means, look for the words “supreme” and “independent”. Options that tie it to one type of state or to how power is misused are traps.

items.hint1: Ask what new feature the Clifford Constitution introduced that Nigeria had not had before.
items.hint2: Colonial control had begun long before 1922, with Lagos annexed in 1861 and amalgamation in 1914. Cultural diffusion, the spread of culture through contact, is not something a constitution sets up.
items.hint3: Two remain. Ask which one the new feature started, and which one was already going on before 1922.
items.solution:
Answer: D. Democracy in Nigeria

The Clifford Constitution of 1922 introduced the elective principle: for the first time, some Nigerians could elect members of the Legislative Council. Lagos elected three members and Calabar one, although only adult men with an income of at least £100 a year could vote. This led to Nigeria’s first political party, Herbert Macaulay’s NNDP, in 1923, so texts credit the constitution with laying the foundation for democracy and party politics in Nigeria.

How to tell: the constitution’s headline feature is the elective principle, and elections are the starting point of democracy.

Why not the others:
A. Colonial control: it had begun long before 1922, so this constitution did not lay its foundation.
B. Cultural diffusion in Nigeria: this is the spread of culture through contact between peoples, not something a constitution set up.
C. Economic exploitation: it was already part of colonial rule and was not what this constitution introduced.

Exam tip: learn one headline feature for each colonial constitution: Clifford 1922, the elective principle; Richards 1946, regionalism; Macpherson 1951, wide consultation and a central Council of Ministers; Lyttelton 1954, federalism. Most questions test that one feature.

items.hint1: The phrase “non-permanent member” only makes sense in a body where some members hold their seats permanently. Ask which body has such seats.
items.hint2: ECOWAS and OPEC treat all their members alike, with no permanent or temporary seats.
items.hint3: Two remain, a world body and a continental body. Which one has a council where five countries never face re-election?
items.solution:
Answer: B. United Nations (UN)

The UN Security Council has 15 members. Five are permanent (the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China) and ten are non-permanent, elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.

How to tell: Nigeria was elected in October 2013 to a non-permanent seat and served on the Security Council for 2014 and 2015. It has held such a seat several times since independence.

Why not the others:
A. ECOWAS: all its members are equal, with no permanent or non-permanent seats.
C. OPEC: all its members are equal, and Nigeria has been a member since 1971.
D. African Union (AU): it has no permanent members, and Nigeria has been a member since the AU was formed in 2002.

Exam tip: “permanent” and “non-permanent” members point to the UN Security Council. Learn the five permanent members, since questions often ask which country is or is not one of them.

items.hint1: Each country gives its legislature its own name. Match the name to the country.
items.hint2: The House of Lords and the House of Commons are the two chambers of the British Parliament.
items.hint3: Two remain. Recall what the US Senate and the US House of Representatives are called together.
items.solution:
Answer: C. Congress

The legislature of the United States is called Congress. It is bicameral, meaning it has two chambers: the Senate, with two senators from each state, and the House of Representatives, whose seats are shared out by population.

How to tell: the two chambers of the US legislature together form Congress.

Why not the others:
A. House of Lords: it is the upper chamber of the British Parliament.
B. House of Commons: it is the lower chamber of the British Parliament.
D. National Assembly: it is the name of Nigeria’s federal legislature, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Exam tip: learn the names of legislatures in pairs with their countries: the USA, Congress; Britain, Parliament; Nigeria, the National Assembly. Options often mix chamber names with whole legislatures, so check whether each option names one chamber or the whole body.

items.hint1: Deregulation means the government removing its controls so that private firms and market forces run an industry. Think about who in Nigeria has protested against it, and what they were worried about.
items.hint2: Greater efficiency is what supporters of deregulation promise, so it is a hoped-for benefit, not a fear.
items.hint3: The options left fall into two groups: harm to the environment and safety, and harm to people’s livelihoods. Which group matches the worries that workers’ unions have raised?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Unemployment

When an industry is deregulated, private firms move in and often cut staff to reduce costs. In Nigerian Government texts, the main fear behind opposition to deregulation, voiced above all by labour unions, is that it will cause job losses, that is, unemployment.

How to tell: the stem asks for the worry behind opposition. Opposition in Nigeria has come mainly from organised labour, and workers’ chief fear is losing their jobs.

Why not the others:
B. Disaster: it is not one of the standard disadvantages of deregulation at this level.
C. Efficiency: it is the main benefit that supporters of deregulation claim, not a fear.
D. Pollution: it is not one of the standard disadvantages of deregulation at this level.

Exam tip: in merits and demerits questions, sort each option: is it a benefit supporters claim, or a harm opponents fear? For deregulation and privatisation, efficiency is usually listed as a benefit, while job losses and higher prices are listed as the fears.

items.hint1: OPEC is a group of countries whose economies depend heavily on selling crude oil. Check each country against that description.
items.hint2: Saudi Arabia and Kuwait were among the five countries that founded OPEC in Baghdad in 1960.
items.hint3: Two African countries remain. Which one depends on crude oil for most of its export earnings?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Uganda

OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, brings together countries that earn much of their income from exporting crude oil. Its five founders in 1960 were Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. Uganda is not a member.

How to tell: Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are founding members, and Nigeria joined in 1971. Uganda has not joined.

Why not the others:
A. Saudi Arabia: it is a founding member and one of the largest oil producers in OPEC.
B. Nigeria: it joined in 1971 and is one of OPEC’s main African members.
C. Kuwait: it is a founding member of 1960.

Exam tip: when an OPEC question asks for the non-member, check the African options first. Nigeria, Algeria, Libya, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Congo are members, so another African country is likely to be the odd one out.

items.hint1: Read the phrase carefully: Africa is the centrepiece of Nigeria’s foreign policy. Ask what is being placed at the centre of what.
items.hint2: One option makes no sense as a foreign policy aim, and another describes domination, which Nigeria’s policy rejects, since it respects the independence of other African states.
items.hint3: Two remain. Test each against what Nigeria has actually done for Africa: funding the fight against apartheid, supporting liberation movements and sending peacekeepers.
items.solution:
Answer: D. Nigeria pays more attention to Africa’s problems

“Africa as the centrepiece” means that Nigeria gives African affairs first place in its foreign policy. Since independence, Nigeria has shown this by supporting the end of colonial rule, fighting apartheid in South Africa, sending peacekeepers, for example through ECOMOG, and giving aid to other African states.

How to tell: the phrase puts Africa at the centre of Nigeria’s foreign policy, so the matching belief is that Nigeria gives priority to Africa’s problems.

Why not the others:
A. Nigeria can escape border traffics in Africa: this has nothing to do with the policy and makes no sense as its aim.
B. Nigeria is the center of Africa: it turns the phrase around, since the policy puts Africa at the centre of Nigeria’s foreign policy, not Nigeria at the centre of Africa.
C. Nigeria can control Africa: it describes domination, while the policy is based on respect for the independence of other African states.

Exam tip: before reading the options, say the policy phrase in your own words. Then beware of options that reuse a word from the stem, such as “centre”, but change its meaning.

items.hint1: Ask where power sits: all at the centre, shared between levels, or kept mostly by the member units.
items.hint2: A republic is a state whose head is elected rather than born into the post, so the term says nothing about where power is placed.
items.hint3: Of the three left, two share power in some way between the centre and the units. Which one does not share it?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Unitary

In a unitary system, all constitutional power belongs to the central government. Local or regional units may exist, but they get their powers from the centre, which can change or take those powers back.

How to tell: the stem says all constitutional powers are concentrated at the centre, which is the defining feature of a unitary system, as in Britain or Ghana.

Why not the others:
A. Confederal: the member states keep most power and the centre is weak.
B. Federal: the constitution divides power between the centre and the states or regions.
C. Republican: it describes a state with an elected head, not how power is shared between levels.

Exam tip: link the key phrase to the system: “concentrated at the centre” means unitary, “divided” or “shared” means federal, and “weak centre” with units keeping their sovereignty means confederal.

items.hint1: The question asks for the name of a right. Check which options name a right and which name a group of people, an event or a process.
items.hint2: The electorate is the group of people entitled to vote, and registration is the process of putting voters on the register.
items.hint3: Two remain. Ask which one names something a person has, and which names something that takes place.
items.solution:
Answer: B. Franchise

Franchise, also called suffrage, is the right to vote. Many Government texts extend it to the right to vote and be voted for. In Nigeria, citizens aged 18 and above have this right, which is called universal adult suffrage.

How to tell: the stem asks for the name of a right, and the right to vote is the franchise.

Why not the others:
A. Contest: it is a competition between candidates for a post, not a right.
C. Registration: it is the process of enrolling qualified voters on the register.
D. Electorate: it is the group of people who are entitled to vote, not the right itself.

Exam tip: separate the right from the people and the process: franchise or suffrage is the right, the electorate is the people who hold it, and registration is how they get on the list.

items.hint1: The civil service has ranks from junior officers up to the head of a ministry’s career staff. Think about who sits at the top in a ministry.
items.hint2: A principal officer is in the middle ranks, well below the heads of departments.
items.hint3: Of the three left, two head or help to run a single department. Which one is above all the departments in a ministry?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Permanent Secretary

The Permanent Secretary is the most senior career civil servant in a ministry. He or she heads the administrative class, the highest class of the civil service, runs the ministry day to day, advises the minister and is its accounting officer. Above all the Permanent Secretaries sits the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, but that post is not an option here.

How to tell: in a ministry, directors head departments and report to the Permanent Secretary, who reports to the minister.

Why not the others:
B. Director: heads one department and reports to the Permanent Secretary.
C. Assistant Director: ranks below a director.
D. Principal Officer: a middle-level rank, well below the directors.

Exam tip: learn the two heads of a ministry: the minister is the political head, appointed by the President, and the Permanent Secretary is the administrative head, a career civil servant. Many questions test the difference.

items.hint1: This question is about the early 1800s in the far north of what is now Nigeria. Separate the person who started and led the movement from the people who helped him or ruled after him.
items.hint2: The jihad began in 1804 as a movement to reform Islam and remove Hausa rulers seen as unjust. Several members of one family took part, but only one of them called the jihad and was accepted as its commander.
items.hint3: Nana Asma'u was a poet and teacher, so set her aside. Of the three men left, two were a brother and a son who fought under the leader and took over parts of the caliphate after his death in 1817. Which man did they follow?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Usman dan Fodio

Usman dan Fodio was a Fulani Islamic scholar who began the jihad in 1804 to reform Islam and remove the Hausa rulers he saw as unjust. His victories brought the Hausa states under one Islamic government, the Sokoto Caliphate, with emirs ruling each emirate under the caliph.

How to tell: the question asks who led the jihad. Dan Fodio declared it and was accepted as its leader, with the title Amir al-Mu'minin, meaning commander of the faithful. The other people named worked under him or ruled after him.

Why not the others:
B. Nana Asma'u: she was his daughter, a poet and teacher who spread learning, especially among women, but she did not lead the jihad.
C. Abdullahi Fodio: he was dan Fodio's younger brother and a commander under him, and later ruled the western part of the caliphate from Gwandu.
D. Muhammad Bello: he was dan Fodio's son and a commander under him, and after 1817 he ruled from Sokoto as the first Sultan and built up its administration.

Exam tip: in Sokoto Caliphate questions, separate the founder from those who came after. Usman dan Fodio led the jihad; Muhammad Bello ruled from Sokoto and Abdullahi from Gwandu after him.

items.hint1: The reform the syllabus teaches is the one that gave the whole country a single, uniform pattern of local government for the first time. Think about which government carried it out.
items.hint2: That reform was carried out by a military government, and the constitution that followed it recognised local government as a tier of government. Ask which military government prepared Nigeria for a return to civilian rule.
items.hint3: Two of the years fall in the Fourth Republic, when local government was already written into the constitution. Of the two earlier years, which one fell under the Murtala and Obasanjo government rather than at the end of the Second Republic?
items.solution:
Answer: A. 1976

The 1976 Local Government Reform, made by the Murtala and Obasanjo military government, set up a uniform single-tier local government system across Nigeria. It made local government the third tier of government, below the federal and state governments, with elected councils and a share of federal revenue.

How to tell: before 1976, local government differed from region to region, with native authorities in the North and different council systems in the South. The 1976 reform replaced these with one pattern for the whole country, and the 1979 Constitution then recognised local government as a tier. In the syllabus this is the landmark reform, though a further reform followed in 1989.

Why not the others:
B. 1983: this is the year the Second Republic ended in a military coup on 31 December, not the year of the reform.
C. 1999: this is the year of the Fourth Republic constitution and the return to civilian rule, not the local government reform.
D. 2003: this was a Fourth Republic election year, long after the 1976 reform had set the pattern.

Exam tip: for Nigerian local government questions, anchor on 1976: the uniform single-tier system, local government as the third tier, and the Murtala and Obasanjo government. The 1989 reform under Babangida is the next date to know.

items.hint1: Ask which body of rules sets up the arms of government and gives them their powers. Every other law is made under the powers it hands out.
items.hint2: A supreme law is the one that other laws must agree with. If another law clashes with it, the courts can declare that other law void.
items.hint3: Court decisions and military orders are both made by bodies that get their power from somewhere else. Between Acts of Parliament and the one option left, which one creates the legislature itself and limits what it may pass?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Constitution

A constitution is the body of basic rules that sets up the arms of government, shares out their powers and protects citizens' rights. Because other laws are made under the powers it gives, it stands above them.

How to tell: Section 1 of the 1999 Constitution says the Constitution is supreme and binds all authorities and persons in Nigeria. It also says that any other law that goes against it is void to the extent that it goes against it.

Why not the others:
A. Acts of Parliament: laws passed by the legislature are made under the Constitution, and the courts can declare them void if they clash with it.
C. Judicial Precedent: earlier court decisions guide later judges, but the courts themselves must follow the Constitution.
D. Decrees: these are laws made by military governments, and they are not the supreme law under Nigeria's present civilian constitution.

Exam tip: when a question asks for the supreme, highest or fundamental law of a country with a written constitution, the answer is the constitution. Acts, court decisions, customs and decrees are sources of law that sit beneath it.

items.hint1: Think about what could go wrong if one person or one body made the laws, carried them out and judged cases all at once.
items.hint2: Montesquieu argued that people's freedom is at risk when the same hands make, carry out and judge the law. Separation of powers is his answer to that danger.
items.hint3: Weakening one arm or placing one arm above the others would undo the balance the idea is built on, so set those aside. Of the two left, does the doctrine aim to build up one arm, or to stop power being misused?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Preventing abuse of power

Separation of powers means the work of government is shared among three arms: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out and the judiciary interprets them. Keeping them apart, with each able to check the others, stops power from piling up in one set of hands, where it could be used to oppress people.

How to tell: the idea comes from Montesquieu, who wrote that there can be no liberty where the same person or body holds all three powers. Nigeria's 1999 Constitution gives legislative, executive and judicial powers to separate arms for this reason: to protect citizens from arbitrary rule.

Why not the others:
A. Strengthening the executive: the doctrine limits the executive, for example through legislative oversight and judicial review, rather than building it up.
C. Weakening the judiciary: the doctrine protects the courts' independence so that they can check the other arms.
D. Giving supremacy to the legislature: putting any one arm above the others is the kind of concentration of power the doctrine is meant to prevent.

Exam tip: for questions on the purpose of separation of powers or checks and balances, look for the option about protecting liberty or preventing tyranny and abuse of power. Options that favour or weaken one arm go against the idea of balance.

items.hint1: Government has three arms, and each has one main job. Match the job to the arm named in the question.
items.hint2: The legislature's main job is making laws. Work out the main jobs of the other two arms, the executive and the courts.
items.hint3: Carrying out laws is the executive's main job. Of the two options left that are not about making or carrying out laws, which one would a judge do when settling a case?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Interpretation of laws

The judiciary is the arm of government made up of the courts and judges. Its main job is to say what the law means and apply it to real disputes, so that cases between citizens, or between citizens and the government, are settled by law.

How to tell: match each function to its arm. The legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets them. Judges also decide whether other laws and government actions agree with the constitution.

Why not the others:
A. Execution of laws: carrying out laws is the main job of the executive, such as the President, ministers and the police.
B. Law making: this is the main job of the legislature, such as the National Assembly.
D. Appointment of ministers: in Nigeria the President appoints ministers and the Senate confirms them, so this belongs to the executive and the legislature.

Exam tip: learn the three arms as a matching set: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, the judiciary interprets them. Any question on the main function of one arm is solved by this match.

items.hint1: The key word is executive. Some leaders have held the title President only as a ceremonial head, with the real power held by someone else.
items.hint2: An executive president is both head of state and head of government. Nigeria first had one when it moved from the parliamentary system to the presidential system under the 1979 Constitution.
items.hint3: Tafawa Balewa was Prime Minister, not President, so set him aside. Of the three left, ask which one held the title President under the 1979 Constitution, not under the 1963 Republican Constitution or as a military ruler.
items.solution:
Answer: C. Shehu Shagari

An executive president is both head of state and head of government, holding real power to run the government. Nigeria first had one under the 1979 Constitution, which replaced the parliamentary system with the presidential system.

How to tell: Shehu Shagari of the National Party of Nigeria (NPN) won the 1979 presidential election and was sworn in on 1 October 1979 as the first President under the new system. He held office until the military coup of 31 December 1983.

Why not the others:
A. Nnamdi Azikiwe: he became President in 1963, but under the parliamentary system that post was ceremonial, and real power lay with the Prime Minister.
B. Olusegun Obasanjo: he ruled from 1976 to 1979 as military Head of State and handed over to Shagari; he became an elected executive President only in 1999.
D. Tafawa Balewa: he was Prime Minister, the head of government in the First Republic, and never held the title President.

Exam tip: separate ceremonial from executive. In Nigeria's First Republic the President was ceremonial and the Prime Minister held power; from 1979 one executive President held both roles. For any question on the first holder of an office, start from the date the office was created.

items.hint1: Think about which body registers voters, fixes election dates and announces results, and why it needs to stand apart from the parties and the government in power.
items.hint2: The body that runs elections is a commission set up by the constitution. It is meant to be independent, because the party in government also contests the elections.
items.hint3: The National Assembly makes laws and the Presidency runs the government, so neither can fairly referee an election. Of the two commissions left, think about what each one looks after: government workers, or voters and candidates.
items.solution:
Answer: B. INEC

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is the body the 1999 Constitution sets up to organise and conduct elections in Nigeria. It is meant to be independent so that no party or arm of government can control the result.

How to tell: INEC registers voters and political parties, fixes election dates, runs the voting and announces the results of presidential, National Assembly, governorship and State House of Assembly elections. Local government elections in the states are run by each state's own electoral commission.

Why not the others:
A. National Assembly: it makes laws, including the Electoral Act that guides elections, but it does not run them.
C. The Presidency: it heads the executive, and a government whose party contests elections cannot fairly run them.
D. Civil Service Commission: it handles the appointment, promotion and discipline of civil servants, not elections.

Exam tip: for questions on which body does what, match the body's name to its job. Electoral commissions run elections, civil service commissions manage government workers, and the legislature makes the rules they both work under.

items.hint1: Nigeria returned to civilian rule in 1979, at the start of the Second Republic. Ask which military ruler was in office on that date.
items.hint2: A leader can hand over power only if he is still in office when the handover happens. Check when each ruler's time in power began and ended.
items.hint3: Gowon was removed in a coup in 1975, and Abacha ruled in the 1990s, so set them aside. Of the two left, which one was still in office in 1979?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Olusegun Obasanjo

Military disengagement means the armed forces leaving government and handing power to elected civilians. In 1979 Nigeria's military government completed a planned transition programme and handed over to the civilian government of the Second Republic.

How to tell: General Olusegun Obasanjo became Head of State after Murtala Mohammed was killed in February 1976. He kept to the transition timetable Murtala had announced, and on 1 October 1979 he handed power to President Shehu Shagari.

Why not the others:
A. Yakubu Gowon: he was removed in a coup in July 1975, years before the handover.
B. Murtala Mohammed: he announced the transition programme but was killed in a failed coup attempt in February 1976.
D. Sani Abacha: he ruled from 1993 until his death in 1998, and the next handover, in 1999, was made by Abdulsalami Abubakar.

Exam tip: learn Nigeria's two military handovers as pairs: 1979, Obasanjo to Shagari, and 1999, Abubakar to Obasanjo. For any leader question tied to a year, first check who was actually in office that year.

items.hint1: Institutions of government have objects linked with them. Ask which object stands for the authority of the house itself, not a tool used in it or something its officers wear.
items.hint2: The object is a ceremonial staff that represents the house's authority. In the syllabus, the house cannot sit lawfully without it in place, which is why seizing it during a quarrel is serious.
items.hint3: Robes are clothing and seals stamp documents, so neither stands for the house itself. Of the two left, one is a small hammer for calling order and one is the ornamental staff. Which is the staff?
items.solution:
Answer: B. The Mace

In Nigeria and other legislatures that follow the British tradition, the mace is an ornamental staff that stands for the authority of the house. It is carried in by an officer called the Sergeant-at-Arms and placed on the table before a sitting begins.

How to tell: in the syllabus, a sitting of the house is not lawful without the mace in place. That is why, when members snatch the mace during a crisis, the sitting has to stop.

Why not the others:
A. The Gavel: this is a small hammer a presiding officer or judge taps to call for order; it is a tool, not the symbol of the house.
C. The Robe: robes are worn by judges, lawyers and some officers of the house, so they mark a person's office, not the authority of the legislature.
D. The Seal: a seal is a stamp used to confirm official documents, such as the seal of the Federation, and does not stand for the legislature.

Exam tip: for symbol-of-authority questions, pair each institution with its object: the mace for the legislature, the gavel as a presiding officer's tool for order, robes and wigs for the courts, and the seal for official documents.

items.hint1: Nigeria's First Republic ran from independence in 1960 to the first military coup in January 1966. Think about which parties were contesting elections in those years.
items.hint2: The main First Republic parties grew out of the nationalist struggle of the 1940s and 1950s, and each had its base in one region. The parties of later republics were formed just before each later return to civilian rule.
items.hint3: The SDP and the NRC were the two parties the Babangida government set up for the Third Republic, so set them aside. Of the two left, which one contested elections before 1966?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Action Group (AG)

Each Nigerian republic had its own set of parties. The First Republic, from 1960 to 1966, was dominated by regional parties: the NPC in the North, the NCNC in the East and the Action Group in the West.

How to tell: the Action Group was founded in 1951 by Obafemi Awolowo and was the main party of the Western Region. It contested the 1959 and 1964 federal elections and formed the opposition in the First Republic parliament. Strictly, it was formed before the First Republic began, but it is the only option that was a First Republic party.

Why not the others:
A. Social Democratic Party (SDP): it was one of the two parties the Babangida government created in 1989 for the Third Republic.
C. People's Democratic Party (PDP): it was formed in 1998 and has been a leading party of the Fourth Republic, which began in 1999.
D. National Republican Convention (NRC): it was the SDP's partner party, also created by the government in 1989 for the Third Republic.

Exam tip: link each republic to its parties. First Republic: NPC, NCNC and AG. Second Republic: NPN, UPN, NPP and others. Third Republic: SDP and NRC. Fourth Republic: PDP, APC and others. Place the party in its era first, then match the republic.
